name: Uber 2015: the new dispatch system (DISCO, S2 geo index, ringpop)
description: Uber's dispatch system after the 2015 rewrite. The driver app reports its location about every 4 s, and the location is written to the "geo index by supply": the earth is split into cells with Google S2, the cell ID is the shard key, and each location goes to the shard that owns it and then to a few replicas. When a rider requests a ride, DISCO (dispatch optimization) first asks the geo index for supply nearby (reads replicas), then asks the routing/ETA service for the arrival time by road, ranks the results and sends the offer to a driver through the Supply service; the Demand service records the rider's demand. The dispatch system is written in Node.js and uses ringpop (a consistent hash ring + SWIM gossip) to shard across thousands of nodes, with some state in Riak. The work after a trip (ratings, email, database updates, payment scheduling) runs in the Python post-trip pipeline; the oldest system uses Postgres. The design target is a million writes per second to the geo index, with several times as many reads. Fan-out lets a node that is sometimes slow raise the tail latency, so TChannel has backup requests (hedged requests) built in. Sources: https://highscalability.com/how-uber-scales-their-real-time-market-platform/ (a write-up of Matt Ranney's talk at QCon London 2015), https://www.infoq.com/presentations/uber-market-platform/ , https://www.uber.com/blog/ringpop-open-source-nodejs-library/ . The parameters are small values for teaching, not Uber's real numbers.

nodes.label: Driver app (reports location every 4 s) + rider app
Geo index (sharded by S2 cell, ringpop)

notes.text: Try it: 1) Run the scenario first: traffic climbs to 3× from second 10, and 70% of it is driver location writes. Each write lands on the primary of one shard and is copied to 2 replicas; the busiest shard reaches about 92%. At second 60, one replica of shard 0 becomes 5× slower: besides answering reads, it must apply every replicated write, so it soon falls behind, its queue fills up, and reads sent to it time out or are rejected; about 3,400 requests fail. 2) Change the geo index to 16 shards (delete the event at second 60 first): the busiest shard drops to about 50%. Only more shards can spread the writes. 3) Change back to 8 shards and set the replicas to 4: the busiest is still about 91%, because more replicas spread only the reads, and each replica must still apply all writes. 4) Put the event at second 60 back and set the geo index's "max acceptable lag" to 500 ms: DISCO skips the replica that falls behind, and failures drop to about 50.

Simplified: the driver and rider apps are combined into one user node, with a read ratio of 30%; a small part of the writes create trips. A real nearby query reads several cells at the same time from the S2 coverage (fan-out); here one read goes to only one shard. ringpop's gossip, forwarding, and rebalancing when nodes join and leave are not simulated. In a data center failure, Uber recovers with the state digest on the drivers' phones; there is no component for that either.
